evidence: When James Brown played Lagos in 1970, Fela invited Brown's band to his club, the Afro-Spot. Bootsy Collins has described hearing Fela's band there as another dimension of the James Brown groove, deeper than he had known, and said he later tried to record those feels with Bootsy's Rubber Band; Tony Allen recalled Brown's musicians coming every night and writing down his patterns. These accounts come from a 1999 Arthur magazine interview with Collins and later interviews, reached here only through search summaries because the pages are blocked from the session. Held at consensus until they are read first-hand.

trackPair.whatToListenFor: Listen for the bass on both. In Fela's band the bass plays a short, repeating figure that leaves lots of space, while the guitars and drums fill in around it. On 'Stretchin' Out', Bootsy's bass is looser and more elastic, but it also sits on one groove for a long time instead of following chord changes. Whether that came from Lagos, as Bootsy says, or from Brown's own band, is exactly what this edge argues about.

explanation: In 1970 James Brown played a concert in Lagos, and Fela invited Brown's band to his club. Brown's bass player, Bootsy Collins, later said that Fela's band played a deeper version of the James Brown groove than he had ever heard. Fela's drummer, Tony Allen, remembered Brown's musicians coming every night and writing down what he played. It is the reverse of the usual story, in which African music simply soaked up American funk. The claim rests on the musicians' own later accounts, which is why it is held at consensus, and why the evidence says what could not be read.
